Harden shim startup-failure record path resolution against a TOCTOU race between Path::canonicalize() and cap_std::fs::Dir::open_ambient_dir() in no_follow_diagnostics_dir (src/shim/mod.rs). An attacker with same-user filesystem race capability could replace the workspace root or an ancestor directory between the two calls. Closing this fully would require capability-based directory handles threaded through from a trusted root rather than re-resolving from a path string, a larger architectural change beyond 124-F scope, and this exact canonicalize-then-open pattern is already used elsewhere in the codebase (e.g. canonicalize_workspace itself). Advisory from 124-F (870B1AFF) Copilot review on PR #349; narrow, same-user-race-only threat model, accepted as a follow-up rather than a 124-F blocker.

Harden shim startup-failure record write against a hard-link attack (src/shim/mod.rs write_startup_failure_record): FollowSymlinks::No plus a regular-file check still accept a pre-created hard link at the leaf path, allowing a process with workspace write access to redirect the append onto a same-filesystem file the operator owns. Validate the opened handle's link count/identity via platform-specific metadata (refuse nlink > 1), or redesign storage to avoid reusing an attacker-provided leaf name entirely (e.g. a fresh per-process/per-timestamp filename). Advisory from 124-F (870B1AFF) Copilot review on PR #349; requires pre-existing workspace write access (same privilege level as many other trusted-workspace-content assumptions already made by the shim/daemon), accepted as a follow-up rather than a 124-F blocker.

Research a CLI-first per-workspace Engram process model. Determine whether each workspace can have exactly one writer/sync process while independent short-lived CLI reader processes query the same workspace without being cancelled, coupled to, or blocked by daemon lifecycle. Evaluate database locking and snapshot consistency, workspace identity and process ownership, IPC versus direct database access, concurrent read/write behavior, Windows and Unix semantics, failure recovery, and observability. Measure effectiveness and resource cost against the current daemon-backed model, define safety invariants for single-writer/multi-reader operation, and recommend whether CLI reads should bypass, coexist with, or coordinate through the daemon. Do not implement until the research establishes a safe architecture.

FOLLOW-UP (post-merge closure of 133-S, PR #377 Copilot review round 5): the remediation recommended in stash entries 28C0E138 and F9D1C495 ("remove 142-F from 133-S's custom_fields.items, then backlogit shipment ship 133-S becomes safe") is INCORRECT and must not be followed as-is. Verified via direct source review of backlogit's own repo (C:\Source\GitHub\backlogit, internal/core/shipment_lifecycle.go): "featureScopeRoots" (line ~1164) discovers a covering feature by walking UP the parent_id chain from EVERY item in the shipment's release scope (its manifest), independent of whether that feature is itself an explicit manifest member; the ShipShipment call site (line ~633-649) then unconditionally invokes "returnUnreleasedFeatureItems" (line ~734) for EVERY feature so discovered. That function force-sets every one of the feature's descendants NOT in the release scope to status queued and CLEARS their parent_id ("returned to backlog after release"), regardless of whether the feature itself is an explicit member. Only the SEPARATE decision to mark the feature itself done/archived is gated on explicit membership (explicitScopeSet check, same file ~line 641 and in collectArchiveCandidateIDs ~line 274). Consequence: removing 142-F from 133-S's manifest would stop 142-F itself from being wrongly force-marked done, but would NOT stop the cascade -- backlogit shipment ship 133-S would still force-requeue-and-detach (clear parent_id on) all 77 of 142-F's descendants outside 133-S's 10-item manifest, corrupting the hierarchy for the other nine as-yet-unshipped 142-F-covering shipments (134-S, 137-S, 139-S, 141-S, etc., per stash 982B0B01/284285B5). This is not unique to 133-S: ANY of the ten shipments partially covering 142-F would hit the identical cascade if it ever calls "backlogit shipment ship" instead of a manual safe-close, regardless of manifest edits. Corrected recommendation for Stage: (1) do NOT treat 'remove 142-F from the manifest' as sufficient to unblock backlogit shipment ship for 133-S or any of its sibling shipments; (2) continue using the manual safe-close path (archive manifest items individually, transition the shipment's own status directly) for every one of the ten 142-F-covering shipments until either backlogit changes returnUnreleasedFeatureItems to skip non-explicit-member features, or 142-F becomes fully covered by whichever shipment ships last; (3) treat this as a workspace-wide multi-shipment coordination risk, not a 133-S-only defect. Source: docs/closure/133-S-2026-09-03-post-merge-closure.md, PR #377 review threads (dbId 3927781997, 3927782075, 3927782151).
